title: Learned Token Pruning for Transformers

problem.claim: Deploying transformer models efficiently is challenging because inference costs, including memory footprint, latency, and power consumption, scale quadratically with input sequence length.

gap.claim: Existing token pruning methods leave room for improved accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and robustness to variations in input sequence length.

contributions.claim: Learned Token Pruning adaptively removes unimportant tokens as an input sequence passes through transformer layers.
The method prunes tokens whose attention scores fall below a layer-specific threshold learned during training, allowing sequence length to vary with the input while avoiding top-k token selection.
The authors implemented the method in PyTorch and open-sourced the code.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present Learned Token Pruning as a novel token reduction method.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On GLUE and SQuAD, the authors report up to approximately 2.5% higher accuracy than prior state-of-the-art token pruning methods at the same FLOPs.
The authors report up to 2.1× FLOPs reduction with less than 1% accuracy drop, along with up to 1.9× throughput improvement on Intel Haswell CPUs and 2.0× on NVIDIA V100 GPUs.
The authors report greater robustness than prior methods to variations in input sequence length.

narrative_sequence.summary: Transformer inference is difficult to deploy efficiently because its costs grow quadratically with input sequence length.
The paper introduces Learned Token Pruning, which adaptively removes unimportant tokens during transformer processing.
LTP uses learned layer-specific attention thresholds to prune tokens and adapt sequence length without top-k selection.
Experiments on GLUE and SQuAD report improved accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, FLOPs reduction, throughput gains, and robustness to input-length variation.
The implementation was developed in PyTorch and open-sourced.

source_observation.claim: The method is reported to reduce FLOPs and improve throughput while keeping the accuracy drop below 1% in the reported setting.

interpretation.claim: Compute reduction can translate into hardware-dependent throughput gains when model accuracy remains near baseline.

application.claim: Evaluate pruning methods using both task accuracy and hardware-specific throughput rather than FLOPs alone.

exception.claim: The reported gains are limited to the abstract's stated tasks, hardware, and evaluation conditions.

unknowns: The abstract does not describe the training procedure or threshold parameterization in detail.
The abstract does not provide baselines, datasets splits, absolute accuracy values, or statistical variation.
The abstract does not report memory or power measurements.
The abstract does not specify the scope or license of the open-source implementation.
